passage: Lavanya's Nani would turn seventy on Sunday, and at the village anganwadi the teacher pinned up a sample card: a pink flower on a tall stem. Lavanya chewed her crayon. Hrithik, beside her, was already drawing a tractor. First she drew a round middle, just like the sample. Then she counted the petals on the wall with her finger and drew the same number. Then came the stem, long and green. She looked at it, frowned, and added a big yellow sun in the corner, rays and all. "Nani likes sun," she told Hrithik. Hrithik nodded and put a sun over his tractor too.

qa.q: What did Lavanya add in the corner of her card?
qa.a: She added a big yellow sun in the corner, rays and all.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya frown and then add the sun?
qa.a: She seemed unsatisfied with a card that only matched the sample and wanted it to feel like her own gift for Nani; she looked pleased once the sun was there.

qa.q: What else could Lavanya try if she wants a card that looks less like everyone else's?
qa.a: She could try a doodle of her own on scrap paper first, or ask the teacher how to draw something Nani loves; copying gave her a start, and those could make it even more personal.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Lavanya's idea?
qa.a: Hrithik liked the sun enough to put one over his own tractor, so her change gave him a new idea too.

grounding: Shows a child copying the teacher's sample flower step by step and then changing it by adding her own sun.

passage: It was raining in Lisbon, and the kindergarten smelled of wet coats. Abebe's birthday was tomorrow, so Ms Duarte put a sample card on each table: a red flower on a thin stem. Valentina pressed her nose close to it. Step one: a red circle. Step two: petals, one, two, three, four, five, all touching the circle. Step three: the stem. It looked just like the teacher's, and that was a little boring. So she grabbed orange and drew a sun with a smiley face above the flower. "Abebe's sun," she whispered, and slid the card into her bag before anyone could see.

qa.q: Where did Ms Duarte put the sample cards?
qa.a: Ms Duarte put a sample card on each table.

qa.q: What does Valentina's whisper and hiding the card suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seemed proud of her own smiley sun and excited to keep the card a surprise for Abebe's birthday.

qa.q: Which approach might suit Valentina if she wants a card that looks nothing like the sample next time?
qa.a: She could picture her own design first or try a few doodles on scrap paper; the sample was a good start because she changed it.

qa.q: What might it be like for Abebe to get this card?
qa.a: Abebe would get a flower like everyone's, but with a sun made just for this birthday, so it might feel more personal than a plain copy 😊

grounding: Illustrates copying a teacher's sample flower as a starting point and then changing it by adding a personal sun.

passage: Maria had one clean sheet left, and the party was at four. Her first card lay ruined on the table: glitter glue had run into the cat she drew, and her fingers had dragged it into a silver smear. Maria's lip wobbled. Sarita, her big cousin, said, "Only one more paper, Maria." Maria sat very still. Then she picked up a pencil, not the glue. She drew the cat lightly, then the words "Happy Birthday" in pencil too. Only when that was done did she squeeze glitter, carefully, around the edges like a frame. Nothing smeared this time.

qa.q: How many clean sheets did Maria have left?
qa.a: Maria had one clean sheet left.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she looked at her first card?
qa.a: Her wobbling lip shows she was upset and disappointed that the glitter glue had smeared her cat.

qa.q: What else could Maria try to keep the glitter from spoiling a drawing?
qa.a: She could let the glitter dry before touching the card or keep her hand on a scrap sheet; drawing first and adding glitter last already solved most of it.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Maria's second try?
qa.a: Sarita had warned there was only one paper, so she might feel relieved and impressed that Maria slowed down and got it right.

grounding: Shows a child learning from a smeared glitter mess to draw in pencil first and add glitter only around the border.

passage: In their Pune flat, Neelam was making a card for Sarika from the fourth floor. She drew a big cake and squeezed gold glitter glue on the candles straight away. When she reached for a crayon to colour the cake, her wrist swept through the wet gold. The cake turned into a shiny blur. "Mamma, it's spoiled!" Neelam looked at the mess, then at her sparkly wrist. "The sparkly goes last," she decided. She took a fresh page, drew the cake in pencil, coloured it, and put glitter only around the edge. This time she kept her hand far away while it dried.

qa.q: What did Neelam use to draw the cake on the fresh page?
qa.a: She drew the cake in pencil, then coloured it.

qa.q: What does Neelam's cry of 'it's spoiled' show about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt upset and frustrated when her wrist turned the cake into a shiny blur.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were helping Neelam next time?
qa.a: Keep the glitter glue out of reach until the drawing and colouring are done, which is the order she worked out herself.

qa.q: What would change for Sarika if Neelam had given up after the first card?
qa.a: Sarika would have got no card at all, or a blurry one; because Neelam changed the order, Sarika gets a neat cake with a gold edge.

grounding: Illustrates a child using a glitter smudge as a lesson to draw in pencil first and add glitter only at the border.

passage: Chen knelt at the kitchen table in their Vancouver apartment with a blue marker and a folded card for Leila. He had drawn a dog. The words were the hard part. "Mom, how do you write Happy Birthday?" Mom wrote it in big letters on a notepad. Chen put his finger under the H. He made an H. Finger on the A. He made an A. The two Ps came out a bit wobbly. Letter by letter he got to the end, then held the card up next to Mom's page. "Same!" Mom grinned. The Y was backwards, but Leila wouldn't mind.

qa.q: What had Chen drawn on the card?
qa.a: He had drawn a dog.

qa.q: How can you tell Chen felt proud at the end?
qa.a: He held the card next to Mom's page and shouted 'Same!', which shows he felt proud and delighted to have written it himself 😊

qa.q: What else could Chen try once he knows a few more letters?
qa.a: He could sound the words out and ask Mom to check afterwards, so he leans a little less on copying each letter.

qa.q: How might Mom see the backwards Y?
qa.a: Mom grinned instead of correcting it, so she seems to care more about the effort than a perfect letter.

grounding: Shows a child asking a parent to spell a birthday greeting and copying the letters one by one from her page.

passage: The clinic waiting room was full, and Parveen's number was still far away. Ammi had brought paper and crayons. "I'll make Gopika's card," Parveen said. Gopika lived next door and her party was tomorrow. Parveen drew a balloon, then stopped. "Ammi, how do you write Happy Birthday?" Ammi wrote it slowly on the back of the clinic slip. Parveen copied the H, then looked up. Then the A. A nurse called another number; Parveen didn't even hear. By the time her own number came, every letter was on the card, and she was beaming.

qa.q: Where did Ammi write the words for Parveen?
qa.a: Ammi wrote it slowly on the back of the clinic slip.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when every letter was on the card?
qa.a: She was beaming, so she felt happy and proud that she had written it herself.

qa.q: Which other approach could Parveen use if Ammi were busy?
qa.a: She could copy the words from a card or poster nearby, or tell the message with a picture; asking Ammi worked because Parveen can't spell it yet.

qa.q: How might the long wait look to Ammi?
qa.a: For Ammi, the card turned a slow, crowded wait into a calm, busy time for Parveen, which probably made the waiting easier.

grounding: Illustrates a child asking her mother to spell a greeting and copying it letter by letter because she cannot yet spell it.

passage: Note, Tuesday, Sunflower class. Ishita worked hard this morning on a card for Sangeeta's birthday. She drew a house, but the roof tilted and one wall leaned. She stared at it, crushed the paper into a ball, and said, "It's ugly." I offered a new sheet and she shook her head, arms folded. "I'm not making one." She sat under the table for a while. At circle time Sangeeta got cards from the others; Ishita watched and looked at the floor. Tomorrow I will draw something wobbly myself, to show her that mistakes are allowed, and I'll tell her mother at pickup today.

qa.q: What did Ishita draw for Sangeeta's card?
qa.a: She drew a house, but the roof tilted and one wall leaned.

qa.q: What might Ishita have been feeling as Sangeeta got the other cards?
qa.a: Looking at the floor suggests she felt sad and maybe ashamed that she had nothing to give after crushing hers.

qa.q: What else could Ishita try when a drawing comes out crooked?
qa.a: She could keep the crooked house and add to it, or try again on the new sheet; wanting it perfect is what made her stop.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Ishita's giving up?
qa.a: The note-writer sees that fear of a crooked result stopped her, and plans to draw something wobbly on purpose so she learns mistakes are allowed.

grounding: Shows a child crumpling a crooked drawing and refusing to try again, so the wish for a perfect card stops the effort.

passage: Dhruv bhaiya's birthday was today, and Preeti wanted her card ready before the school bus dropped him at the kasba stand. She sat on the charpai in the courtyard and drew a kite. The string came out bent and the kite was lopsided. Preeti looked at it, scrunched it tight, and threw it by the buffalo trough. "It's ugly." Dadi held out another page from an old notebook. Preeti turned her face away. "No more." When Dhruv came home, he got a laddoo from Dadi and a hug from Maa, but nothing from Preeti. She hid behind the door, wishing she had kept the bent kite.

qa.q: Where did Preeti throw the crumpled card?
qa.a: She threw it by the buffalo trough.

qa.q: What does Preeti hiding behind the door suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seems sorry and a bit ashamed, wishing she had kept the bent kite so she had something to give Dhruv.

qa.q: What would you change first for Preeti?
qa.a: Help her see that a lopsided kite is still a gift, or gently get her to try Dadi's fresh page; one more go could have left her with a card.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see getting nothing from Preeti?
qa.a: Dhruv doesn't know about the bent kite, so he might only notice that his little sister is hiding and wonder why.

grounding: Illustrates a child crumpling a crooked drawing and refusing another try, so the wish for perfection leaves her with no card.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof, so all twenty children were stuck inside the playschool, and there was only one red toy car. Kishore and Jasleen both had a hand on it. "Mine!" "I had it first!" Jasleen let go and ran to Miss Rekha. Miss Rekha came over and knelt down. "Kishore, tell me." He said he'd found it in the box. "Jasleen?" She said she had only put it down to fix her shoe. Miss Rekha nodded at both. "So what can we do?" After a moment, Kishore pushed the car to the middle of the mat. They drove it together, one pushing, one catching.

qa.q: Why were all the children stuck inside?
qa.a: Rain drummed on the tin roof, so they were stuck inside the playschool.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen let go and run to Miss Rekha?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and unfairly treated, since she had only put the car down to fix her shoe, and she trusted the teacher to sort it out.

qa.q: What else could Kishore and Jasleen try before running to a teacher next time?
qa.a: They could agree to take turns or push it together from the start, which is where they ended up anyway.

qa.q: What is it like for Miss Rekha to settle quarrels on a rainy day?
qa.a: With twenty children indoors and one red car, Miss Rekha has to listen patiently to both sides, which takes time but keeps things calm.

grounding: Shows a child running to the teacher over a toy car, and the teacher listening to both children and helping them agree.

passage: The wind-up car had one key, and at the Chennai playschool both Gargi and Yamini wanted to turn it. Gargi grabbed; Yamini grabbed back. Then Yamini ran across the room. "Aunty! Gargi took the car!" The teacher came and held the car up high. "One at a time. Gargi?" "I wanted to wind it." "Yamini?" "I wanted to wind it!" The teacher smiled. "So you both want to wind it. What's fair?" Yamini thought. "She winds, I race it. Then I wind." Gargi nodded. The car zoomed across the floor twice, and nobody cried.

qa.q: How many keys did the wind-up car have?
qa.a: The wind-up car had one key.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she ran to the teacher?
qa.a: She felt upset and cross that Gargi had taken the car, and hoped the teacher would make it fair.

qa.q: Which other approach might suit Gargi and Yamini once they're a little older?
qa.a: They could bargain by themselves, like 'she winds, I race it', without waiting for an adult; the teacher's question showed them how.

qa.q: How does the teacher see the quarrel?
qa.a: The teacher sees that both simply want to wind the car, and helps them notice it so they can find a fair split.

grounding: Illustrates children asking the teacher to settle a quarrel over a toy car, with the adult listening to both and helping them agree.

passage:
"Give it!"
"No, it's mine! Nani gave it to me!"
"She gave it to both of us!"
Mehak and Dhruv were pulling the tin spinning top back and forth across the sofa.
"Children!" Papa called from the kitchen. "Too loud!"
Dhruv's face went red. "I want it NOW."
Mehak stopped pulling. She looked at the clock, then at the top.
"Okay. You have it now, I have it after lunch."
"All of after lunch?"
"Till the cartoons start."
Dhruv thought. "Deal."
He spun it on the floor. Mehak went to help Papa with the rotis, and the house went quiet.

qa.q: Who gave the spinning top?
qa.a: Nani gave it.

qa.q: Why did Mehak stop pulling and look at the clock?
qa.a: She seems tired of the fight and eager to end it, so she thought about time and found a way for each of them to get a turn.

qa.q: What could make Mehak's deal even clearer next time?
qa.a: Settle the exact end of each turn before agreeing; she already did this when Dhruv asked 'All of after lunch?' and she said until the cartoons start.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa once the deal is made?
qa.a: Papa was bothered by the shouting, so the quiet house and Mehak coming to help with the rotis probably felt like a relief.

grounding: Shows a child ending a shouting match by offering a split: the other child gets the toy now and she gets it after lunch.

passage: Daycare note, Thursday. Eshaan and Vandana both wanted the big dump truck in the sand pit this morning. Voices rose fast; Vandana was crying and Eshaan was shouting. Before I reached them, Eshaan held the truck out and said, "You have it now, I have it after lunch." Vandana stopped crying and took it. After lunch, Eshaan went straight to the sand pit and waited. Vandana handed it over without a word. I praised both of them for keeping the deal. I'm sharing this so families can use the same words at home when toys cause shouting.

qa.q: Where did Eshaan and Vandana want the dump truck?
qa.a: They both wanted the big dump truck in the sand pit.

qa.q: How can you tell Vandana felt calmer after the offer?
qa.a: Vandana stopped crying and took the truck, which suggests the offer made Vandana feel relieved and sure of a turn.

qa.q: What could the caregiver do to help this kind of deal happen more often?
qa.a: Teach other children the same 'now and after lunch' words and praise deals that are kept, which the note already starts doing.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Eshaan's idea?
qa.a: The note-writer sees it as a simple way to end shouting and thinks it is worth passing on to families to use at home.

grounding: Illustrates a child splitting time with a toy, now for one and after lunch for the other, which ends the shouting.

passage: Teacher's note, Monday. At snack time Anand knocked down Indu's block tower. Indu moved to the far corner and sat with her knees up. When I asked if she wanted to play, she said, "If he says sorry, then I forgive him. Not before." She said it three times through the morning, very firmly. Anand kept looking over but didn't come. They didn't play together outdoors either, which they always do. Just before home time, Anand walked over and mumbled sorry. Indu jumped up at once. Tomorrow I'll talk with them both about other ways to fix a fight.

qa.q: What did Anand knock down?
qa.a: Anand knocked down Indu's block tower.

qa.q: Why did Indu keep repeating her rule all morning?
qa.a: She felt hurt that her tower was knocked down and wanted Anand to show he was sorry before she felt okay playing again.

qa.q: What else could Indu try instead of waiting all morning?
qa.a: She could tell Anand how the fallen tower made her feel, or ask him to help rebuild it; her rule was clear but kept them apart all day.

qa.q: How does the teacher see Indu's rule?
qa.a: The teacher notices the rule was firm but kept the two apart for the whole morning, and plans to show them other ways to fix a fight.

grounding: Shows a child's firm rule, forgiving only after a sorry, keeping a quarrel going until the other child apologises.

passage: Deepak had stepped on Lalremsiami's paper boat by the stream behind the village school, and now it lay flat in the mud. She picked it up and walked home past the pig pen, cheeks hot. At dinner she thought it over. If he says sorry, I'll forgive him. If he doesn't, I won't. It seemed very fair. Next morning Deepak waved from his gate. She looked straight ahead. At lunch he held out a guava. She shook her head: no sorry, no guava. All day she played alone. Near evening, Deepak came with a new paper boat. "Sorry," he said. She took it and ran with him to the stream.

qa.q: What did Deepak hold out at lunch?
qa.a: He held out a guava.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami refuse the guava?
qa.a: She still felt hurt about her flattened paper boat and was sticking to her rule of forgiving only after a sorry, even though it left her alone all day.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami have tried, and why?
qa.a: She could have told Deepak she was upset about the boat, or taken the guava as a first step; her rule was fair but rigid, so a whole day was lost.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen her silence?
qa.a: Deepak waved and brought a guava, so her silence may have confused him until he worked out that a sorry and a new boat were needed.

grounding: Illustrates a child's rigid if-then rule, forgiving only after a sorry, which drags the quarrel on through a whole day.

passage: I was drying clothes on our balcony when Eshaan and Aadhya had their fight in the lane below. It was over the chalk, I think. Aadhya said something sharp and Eshaan's face crumpled. Then he did a strange thing: he turned his back and started hopping on the hopscotch squares alone, as if nothing had happened. Aadhya called, "Eshaan? Eshaan!" He kept hopping. She tried once more, then sat on the step, puzzled, rolling the chalk between her hands. Later Eshaan went home early, dragging his feet. I can't say what he was thinking, but it didn't look like the fight had gone anywhere.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do after turning his back?
qa.a: He started hopping on the hopscotch squares alone.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been feeling as he went home dragging his feet?
qa.a: His crumpled face and dragging feet suggest he still felt hurt and low; pretending the fight wasn't there didn't make the feeling leave.

qa.q: What else could Eshaan try instead of pretending the fight wasn't there?
qa.a: He could tell Aadhya that her words hurt, or ask a grown-up to help them talk; turning away just left both of them stuck.

qa.q: How does Aadhya seem to experience Eshaan's silence?
qa.a: Aadhya called his name and then sat on the step, so she seems puzzled and shut out, not sure what happened.

grounding: Shows a child turning away and acting as if a fight never happened, leaving the hurt in place and the other child puzzled by the silence.

passage:
Monday. In the school corridor, Omkar grabbed the front spot in the train line. "You're a baby, you can't be driver." Yash turned to the wall and hummed loudly, as if Omkar had vanished.
Tuesday. Omkar held out a clay snake. "Want to make a snake farm?" Yash stared at the ceiling fan and said nothing. Omkar scratched his head and wandered off.
Thursday. At recess Omkar drove a train of three other boys around the slide. Yash sat on the bench with his lunchbox, not eating. When the teacher asked what was wrong, he shrugged. Monday's words were still stuck inside him.

qa.q: What did Omkar offer on Tuesday?
qa.a: He held out a clay snake and asked if Yash wanted to make a snake farm.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling on the bench on Thursday?
qa.a: Not eating and shrugging suggest he still felt hurt and lonely; ignoring Monday's words hadn't made them go away.

qa.q: What would you change first for Yash?
qa.a: Instead of humming and staring away, he could tell Omkar or the teacher that being called a baby hurt, so the fight could actually be sorted out.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Yash's silence on Tuesday?
qa.a: Omkar scratched his head and wandered off, so he seems puzzled and may not even know his words hurt.

grounding: Illustrates a child pretending a fight is not there over several days, while the hurt stays and the other child is left puzzled.

passage:
"It's my turn on the swing!"
"No, mine!"
Arohi and Sudha were both holding the chain. Their cousin Tenzin wandered over with a coin.
"Heads, Arohi. Tails, Sudha. Okay?"
"...Okay."
The coin spun. Tails. Arohi pouted but let go, and Sudha swung high.
Two days later, the same two were fighting over the last mango ice lolly.
"Mine!"
"I saw it first!"
Arohi stopped. "Wait. Tenzin's coin way. Heads me, tails you?"
Sudha blinked. "Okay."
Nani flipped a coin for them. Heads. Arohi grinned, and broke off the end for Sudha anyway.

qa.q: What was the second quarrel about?
qa.a: They were fighting over the last mango ice lolly.

qa.q: Why did Arohi stop and suggest the coin the second time?
qa.a: She remembered how the coin had ended the swing fight, even when she lost, and felt hopeful it could stop this one too.

qa.q: What could Arohi and Sudha try when there's no coin around?
qa.a: They could take turns or share, like Arohi did with the end of the lolly; the coin works because both of them accept it as fair.

qa.q: What is the coin idea like from Sudha's side?
qa.a: Sudha agreed at once both times, so the toss seems fair to Sudha, and this time Sudha even got a piece after losing.

grounding: Shows a child learning a coin toss from another child and suggesting it herself at the next quarrel.

passage: Playgroup note, week 3. Wednesday: Deepak and Farhan both wanted the blue scooter and started shoving. Before I could step in, Jomol took a toy coin from the play shop. "Shiny side Deepak, plain side Farhan." Both boys agreed. Plain side. Deepak scowled but waited his turn. Friday: the two argued again, this time over the stethoscope in the doctor corner. I was on my way over when Deepak said, "Coin! Like Jomol!" He fetched one himself and tossed it. He lost, and still handed the stethoscope over. I've put a small jar of toy coins in the doctor corner.

qa.q: Where did the note-writer put a jar of toy coins?
qa.a: The jar of toy coins went in the doctor corner.

qa.q: What does Deepak handing over the stethoscope after losing suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seems to feel the toss was fair and was content to accept it, even though he lost.

qa.q: What else could help the boys when a quarrel starts?
qa.a: They could also take turns by time, one round each; the coin worked because Deepak remembered it and both trusted it.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see what Deepak did on Friday?
qa.a: The note-writer sees Deepak reusing Jomol's idea on his own and supports it by putting coins where the next quarrel is likely.

grounding: Illustrates a child copying another child's coin-toss idea and using it himself at the next quarrel.

passage: The power had gone out in the building, so Noor and Jahnavi were making shadow puppets on the stairwell wall with Jahnavi's torch. "My turn to hold it!" Noor said. "It's my torch!" Noor yanked, Jahnavi yanked back, and the torch clattered down two steps. Noor shouted, "I'm not your friend anymore!" and stomped up to the fourth floor in the dark, feeling her way along the rail. The shouting stopped. Jahnavi sat alone with the flickering torch, chin trembling. The next evening Noor knocked with a packet of biscuits. They played again, but more quietly, and neither of them mentioned the torch.

qa.q: Where did Noor stomp off to?
qa.a: Noor stomped up to the fourth floor in the dark.

qa.q: Why might Noor have knocked with biscuits the next evening?
qa.a: She probably felt sorry and a little embarrassed about her shout, and wanted to make up without having to say so.

qa.q: What else could Noor try when she's angry about the torch?
qa.a: She could ask for turns or say she's cross, instead of saying she's not a friend; the harsh words ended the game but left a hurt behind.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi experience the next evening's play?
qa.a: After sitting alone with a trembling chin, Jahnavi is glad to play again, but the quieter game shows the friendship still feels a bit bruised.

grounding: Shows a child shouting that the friendship is over and stomping off, which ends the fight but leaves a hurt that lasts till the next day's play.

passage: On the roof of their Guwahati building, Bhupen and Manjula were racing marbles down a cardboard ramp. Manjula's green marble won four times in a row. "You're pushing it!" Bhupen said. "I'm not!" Bhupen kicked the ramp flat and shouted, "I'm not your friend anymore!" He stomped down the stairs so hard his slippers slapped. The roof went quiet. Manjula picked up the squashed ramp and carried it home. The next afternoon Bhupen came up again, hands in his pockets. Manjula was there, building a new ramp. He stood at the edge a long time before she said, "You can hold the tape."

qa.q: Whose marble won four times in a row?
qa.a: Manjula's green marble won four times in a row.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been feeling as he stood at the edge the next afternoon?
qa.a: His hands in his pockets and long wait suggest he felt awkward and sorry, unsure whether Manjula would let him play again.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do next time a game feels unfair?
qa.a: He could ask to check the ramp or take a break to cool down; kicking it and shouting ended the game but hurt the friendship.

qa.q: How might Manjula see Bhupen's outburst?
qa.a: Manjula said she wasn't pushing, so she may have felt hurt and wrongly blamed, yet she still offered him the tape the next day.

grounding: Illustrates a child shouting that they are no longer friends and stomping off, which ends the fight but damages the friendship until the next day's play.
